utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We need to enter closed session to allow the witness to come into court.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning, Mr. Crosland.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Your cross-examination by Mr. Ivetic will continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I would like to try and of move through the questions as quick as possible, but I have been told by the translators that we need to pause between my question and your answers since we both speak many same language and therefore the same interpreter will be interpreting our words. So I apologize to-- for that. I just wanted to bring that to your attention, since I know about it and it's my fault for not trying to pause. I should know better.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will try and help you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, we left off yesterday just before branching off on to a new topic. That topic I wish to explore briefly with you is some follow-up questions about the KLA or UCK, to elaborate or clarify some points. Now, first of all, you spoke yesterday about some pressure or criticism, I think you called it, that you felt when trying to maintain fair and balanced reporting about some of the crimes and activities of the KLA, such as labelling them as terrorists, and that persons wanted to view the conflict in terms of all black or all white. Am I correct that this was even the case in 1998, particularly late 1998?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think it was, sir, and it didn't affect in particular my reporting. I tried to report the facts as I saw them giving due influence to those points that I thought important. There were, as we discussed yesterday, some external factors which are probably not relevant to this particular Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. I have just one more question about that particular aspect of it, to -- to check with you with respect to the nature of some of this criticism or pressure. Would you agree with me that despite the questions about the KLA and their reputation, the international community, specifically the American leadership of Bill Clinton, Richard Holbrooke and Madeleine Albright, had decided there was going to be a regime change in Serbia and the KLA was going to be one of the tools to make this happen. And, Colonel, you should not feel bashful about being bluntly honest to me. As an American, I can take criticisms for my fellow co-nationals. But would you agree with me about that statement?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my own personal view, and I and not obviously the Ministry of Defence for whom I used to work; that was the view that I thought was relevant at the time and still do.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: So I would agree with you, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, with respect to the tacit approval or support that the KLA received from the international community in 1998, once this tacit support was given to the KLA, did you notice that it was followed up with any increased activity or any worsening on the ground in Kosovo and Metohija in late 1998 or early 1999?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As I said yesterday, sir, and I've written I believe in this statement, that from the latter part of 1998, we saw a quantum increase in both supplies, materials, and a range of weaponry that certainly added to their ability to take on or to at least engage the Serbian security forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I believe you've already touched upon the fact that the KLA held 50 per cent of the territory, and then I think you later said they technically controlled 70 per cent of the province, and you also went on to describe your knowledge of the number of brave MUP and VJ officers and men who perished in skirmishes. I would like to ask you whether you would agree that there was a great likelihood that any incursion by any Serb -- legitimate Serb security forces onto this 50 or 70 per cent of the territory held by the KLA risked attack from the KLA,; that is to say, that the KLA could attack any patrol that ventured into this territory during the time period that they held it, obviously?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: With respect, sir, it's a very broad question. Up until mid-August, late August when the Serbian security forces started to properly re-engage with the -- the KLA and to start clearing the three of the main axes, I think, in my opinion, that the Serbian forces could have engaged whenever they wished to engage. Now, whether they were ready to engage or not, obviously, I don't know, because I'm not their commander or was party to their chain of command. They certainly had the -- let's put it this way, the physical attributes and capabilities to engage the KLA at a time when the KLA in -- in my estimation, was not as substantial as it was in the latter part of 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've just said, they got resupplied then, and they had extra capability. As I said yesterday, sir, I don't believe that they ever had the weapon firepower to match the Serbian security forces. The numbers, as we venture to disagree on, is another matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. Would you agree with me that as far as counter-terrorist or anti-terrorist actions are concerned that, based upon your observations, they were -- those actions were carried out only in areas where there was an active presence of -- of terrorist-style attacks by the KLA?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not real little, to be honest. Because the -- the amount of destruction, I would call it, as I've called it in many reports, wanton destruction from burning of houses, petrol stations, other business properties, slaughtering of animals, is not conducive, in my opinion, to trying to gain the hearts and minds of a population that in the beginning, as I said, was probably quite happy for neither force to be in the province. But when villages were consistently damaged and in some cases very badly destroyed, then I believe that the Serbian security forces did cause more people to go at least to -- if not to support but to tacitly support the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I believe you mentioned --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Could I just briefly ask a supplementary question to that. The specific point in that question was whether you agreed that the actions, albeit excessive actions, were confined to areas where there was terrorist activity.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Then I must make it clear, Your Honour. I believe, no. Because the destruction was across the -- the area from Kosovska Mitrovica through Pristina down to Urosevac. That was the major area of operations west of that -- east of that area, there were very for apart from the Podujevo salient as it were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, as far as the activities of the KLA are concerned, did you note a general atmosphere of fear that existed among the non-Albanian population of Kosovo as a result of these activities?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did, sir. As I've said already, the goldfish in the bowl, if I may use that expression, were the Serbian population, many of whom had been in the province for over -- for several centuries. And several of these were isolated villages that were farmers and were getting going about their usual business and had lived happily with the majority of their neighbours, as most of us do, until this political incident happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now help me, if you know. I don't know if you -- if you have this information; but according to my information, Kosovo and Metohija had 1.428 villages or populated settlements. Do you -- are you able to confirm that information?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not precisely no, sir. We discussed this yesterday. I saw between 2 and 300 villages that were attacked, but I would -- I would quite easily recognise that that number is a possibility, yep.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'd like to focus, move our discussion to the activities or the area consisting of Pec, Prizren, Decani, and Djakovica. Would you agree that this region was a key area for both sides, due to the fact that many supply routes came through this area?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Great. And are you familiar with the tactics of the KLA to force persons to be mobilised into their forces, particularly in this area, the Dukagjin operative zone?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I don't quite understand your question, sir. But if you mean that the commander of that area was a -- one of the more strident commanders, then I would agree with that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And did you have knowledge from early 1998 onwards of the KLA killing Albanians perceived to be favourable to the Serbian regime?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was certainly on the intelligence and, as I said, we unfortunately picked up several bodies. Who exactly they were, we didn't -- we don't know, because they were just dumped by the roadside. So we just took them into the various centres for -- for burial or further preparation.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And I believe -- you said you picked some up. Was the -- would you estimate -- I think you had estimated in one of your prior statements, I believe the June 2006 statement that you gave to the Prosecutor, I think you estimated that such killings occurred or such bodies would be found approximately once a week?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would be roughly correct. I mean, at times there was -- there was more; other times there was less. But, yeah, that's a reasonable assessments sir, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think, Mr. Ivetic, the interpreters are still having a problem because there is no clear pause taking place. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I will try.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Again, I apologise, sir. I'm trying to move faster to get you out of here to your other appointments, but we have to cooperate with everyone here.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. All right. Now, as of July 1st, 1998, during that time period, Malisevo was still a major KLA base. Isn't that accurate?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. That's correct, sir, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, in your June 2006 statement, specifically at paragraph 48, I believe that you stated that during the time period when you were detained in Malisevo, which I believe was also July of 1998 - you can direct me if I'm wrong on that - but at that time that you were detained there, you saw between 150 and 200 KLA soldiers in that -- in that settlement?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what is written in my statement, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, you agreed with my colleague yesterday that it is difficult sometimes to identify terrorists, and you also stated that there were about 400 hard-core KLA fighters, and I respect your honesty on that and your position. But I want to ask you a different question. Given that there were 150 to 200 fighters in Malisevo, given that the KLA technically controlled almost 70 per cent of the territory of the province and, as you said, they also blocked or controlled three out of four of the major transport routes and had headquarters in 24 locations, would you concede that the KLA had more numerous forces, perhaps not hard-core fighters, but nonetheless armed in some fashion so as to be able to accomplish all these factors that we have set forth?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see where you're going, sir. All I would say is that I suspect that when - and I'm not blowing my own trumpet at all - but when I was detained there and brought in, there was a show of force to show that they were larger than was thought. I think it was the first time that any defence attache had gone into the major -- that particular major headquarters. There was about 100, 150 people there. Some were armed. They were in bits and pieces of uniform. So I -- I can understand where you're going that 150 here must mean there's more than 400. Well, we've already -- I think, with respect to the Court, we discussed yesterday that the low hundreds, and that's really where I'm prepared to stick at, at the moment, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And, again, my pause is not meant to be interpreted -- now, I have just a couple questions on the KLA, and then we can move on to other topics that are of greater interest to me. Now, first of all, relating to the time period from January 1st, 1998 through the 25th of July, 1998, the information I have is that there were, approximately, 878 terrorist acts committed by the KLA against both civilians and official personnel during that time period, including 210 citizens being kidnapped of which included Serbs, Montenegrins, Albanians, Roma, Muslims, and even one Bulgarian resident of the province. Did you have information relating to such a -- such a vast number of citizens being kidnapped by the KLA whose fate for the most part remained unknown?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think we received, sir, a -- a visual briefing from the Foreign Liaison Service of the VJ, which had a situation map showing the type of instance you are talking about. There wasn't, if I remember rightly, a great deal of detail on the map. And without being rude to the Vojska Jugoslavija, I think some of these incidents may not have been as serious as they have been made out. There were obviously some very serious incidents. Don't get me wrong on that point. But I think the numbers game may have been slightly played up at that particular point, and that's the briefing that I got, if I remember correctly, sir. But I don't wish to underestimate the amount of missing people, which was a continual problem to try and get to -- get to the bottom of on both sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. And during that same time period, did you have information that the majority of the killings; again, I have 108 killings during that seven-month time period of which the majority, 66, were civilians and the rest were official personnel. Did you have similar information relating to that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: The civilian side was, as I said, sir, is always difficult to get to grips with because, unfortunately, these people disappeared into the ground. On security side, one was aware that there were several serious incidents where MUP and particularly in the early days and later on VJ then did have casualties, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Now I'd like to move to that portion of your evidence and testimony dealing with the Serb security forces. First of all, with respect to the PJP, am I accurate that your information relating to the PJP did not include any review of any official documents relating to their organisation and structure?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: As -- as I said yesterday, sir, I was -- I was accredited to the Vojska Jugoslavija. When it became clear that the MUP were heavily engaged in operations in -- in Kosovo, I then requested information from my own internal sources so that I was better informed about what may be on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, I believe you had stated that with respect to the SAJ and the JSO that they numbered about 200 to 300 members each during the time period you were on the ground. What is that based upon? Is that your personal observations or information that you received from these other sources that you have -- that you've already indicated for us?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was based on information I received from outside of -- outside of theatre, as it were, and also we used to see the more specialised units, as I mentioned on at least a couple of occasions, going forward to Malisevo when there may have been a hundred or so grouped together. And having had a history in special forces myself, you start getting thousands of people. They aren't very special and, therefore, they tend to be numbers tend to be fewer, better equipped, and asked to do specific jobs rather than ordinary infantry jobs. So I would be surprised if the numbers were very much higher than what I have put in my report, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And I'd like to move on to some of the other elements or forces that you -- that you testified about. If we could focus for a moment on the forces you identified as Arkan's forces. Did you personally see Arkan's forces in Kosovska Mitrovica or is this also based upon outside of theatre intell or information?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I used to go up to KiM on several occasions as part of scanning through the entire area and Zvecin and was an area where one was not particularly warmly welcomed, because that was one of the basis that I presume they were working out of. There were other instances where, as I indicated in my report, people who were neither military nor -- or MUP, and, therefore, the assumption based on a fairly thorough knowledge and being down there from day-to-day on a daily basis that they were probably of that persuasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: As far as people of this persuasion, were they attired in uniforms?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: There used to be a variety of dress, if I remember rightly. Some may have been wearing battle fatigues and boots, and then a shirt on top. And sometimes that was uniform; sometimes it wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, in your statement, you have -- you have indicated an incident with a photographer, an ITN photographer, I believe. Am I correct this is the only specific instance of a crime or an assault that you witnessed -- that you eyewitnessed these persons of questionable affiliation that you witnessed these persons [Realtime transcript read in error "Americans"] perpetrate during the time you were on the ground?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I think I said in the paragraph concerning -- I can't find it now. These persons were either paramilitary or maybe even RDB. I don't know, but that was the only one we physically witnessed. There were various statements from civilians, which one has to give measured weight to, that they'd been assaulted by paramilitaries, et cetera, et cetera; and bearing in mind these are frightened civilians and, therefore, anyone with arms looking slightly rough and hairy, to be blunt, could be classed as paramilitary.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Right. Now, I believe yesterday, in response to one of the questions from my colleagues, you stated that you could not specifically recall any incidents where army personnel had bandannas. I'd like to ask you the same question with respect to the police. Am I correct that you cannot specifically recall incidents where you saw clearly identified police personnel wearing bandannas around their heads?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, there were -- there were incidents. To ask me specifically, I cannot recall precisely. But after operations, men tend to try and relieve the tensions of having gone into battle. And as I've gone into battle on several occasions, one can understand people slightly showing off, if I may put it that way. And there is an adrenaline rush that is a quite natural occurrence post a fairly difficult and demanding situation. So I think some of the lads, I would say, would be wearing this and would be fairly confident of their ability to overcome the objective of what they were going against. And as a former soldier, one request understand that. There just needs to be some discipline as well as a natural exuberance to get rid of the tensions of having been in a conflict situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I have to correct an item in the transcript at page 12, line 8, in my question about "the persons of questionable affiliation that you witnessed," the transcript says, "these Americans perpetrate." I think I said, "these persons," but I won't take it personally. Okay. Thank you, sir. Now, if we can move on. At paragraph 21 of your 92 ter statement, that's the statement that we're dealing with in case, you describe MUP personnel at check-points being frightened of the danger they were exposed to. Would -- at the time -- since we don't have a time reference for this statement, was the danger that you were referring to from the KLA or from NATO?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, this period, as I said, was in early and late spring 1998. I think this refers to the Drenica area where I toured extensively on a day-to-day basis, and we came across isolated check-points of perhaps five, six, seven, eight MUP scattered around the Drenica area which was, as we all know, one of the key KLA areas. And I used to tour around; and depending on the reception I got, we might have a glass of whisky with people to cheer them up, because it was raining and pretty uncomfortable and they were in isolated positions. And I think, as a soldier, one understands how they feel. So I certainly got the impression that some of the -- some of the MUP quite understandably, and I'm not maligning their military intent. I think anyone who has been in a situation like that if they're not apprehensive and slightly disturbed at the situation they find themselves in, they're not, I would call it, switched on to the situation. So it was a comment on the -- the situation at the time, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I'd like to focus upon your observations relating to the Ponosevac settlement that's described at paragraph 34 of your statement in Djakovica municipality in May of 1998, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yep.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And I would, first of all, ask you do you recall that during the first part of May 1998, there was a police station, a Serbian MUP police station located in Ponosevac that was subject to almost daily attacks by the KLA -- the KLA forces that were surrounding that village?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do, sir. We arrived there right in the middle of one such attack, and I think we even sheltered with the MUP while the attack went on.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, I would like to then move on to another area at paragraph 41 and 42 of your statement when talking about Junik, Prilep, Rznik, and Glodjane. Am I correct that all of these villages were in KLA strongholds; that is to say, areas that the KLA had held for some time in 1998?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: The -- certainly Junik, Glodjane, we know about. Prilep and Rznik were just off the main supply route going from Pec to Gornja Djakovica, and that was a contested area. There was for many months a MUP vehicle check-point there, which was attacked on many occasion, and several MUP I know were killed there. So, yes, it was in the KLA, I wouldn't say control zone. It was a disputed zone between both forces and a particularly difficult place, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: You've mentioned the police point at Prilep. The -- the police point in Prilep was actually being attacked from the KLA that were based in the village from the east in Rznic. Is that accurate from your recollection?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, sir. I mean, that's back towards our friend Ramush's area, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: All right. By the way, by any chance were you among the group of military attaches who were in a convoy on June 7, 1998, that was attacked in this region on the road outside of Prilep?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. My -- our eldest daughter was being married, so the 6th of January I was back in the United Kingdom. But I know the incident you're referring to. When the MUP helped extract the Canadian defence attache, my -- my replacement and a couple of others, I think, in Gornji Streoc.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you talked about the station -- the point in Prilep being attacked multiple times. The information I have is that from July 1, 1998 through the 11th of August, 1998, there were a total of 32 attacks resulting in seven dead policemen and 19 wounded policemen. In any event, these attacks that -- that you and I have been talking about, do you have information that such attacks were being staged by the KLA from within these so-called Kulas, the walled fortifications or houses?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I mean, this is the classical shoot and scoot policy that the KLA began to adapt and were fairly successful at. Because having stood and fought at the Jashari compound in Likosane and Donji Prekaz, they resized that wasn't the tactic to use against very superior forces. And, therefore, any stationary check-point like there was at Prilep along that road from Decani -- Pec-Decani-Djakovica was open to attack, because the MUP had to live in those locations and, therefore, presented targets to snipers, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I don't think that's dealing with the issue. In fact, it sounds as though you're disagreeing with the proposition that Mr. Ivetic put to you. The question was whether they were staging attacks from the Kulas, which is a concept I have difficulty with, and I was going to ask you to explain it further. Can you help?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour. The Kulas, I think my learned friend is referring to are the big walled enclosures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I understand what they are.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Therefore, they were using them as cover to fire at. I mean, we're talking at a range of between 2 and 400 metres from the check-point which snipers could move into and then pick off policemen going about their normal duties in what was a very isolated vehicle check-point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, if we can move to another area. First of all, you -- you have clarified for us that you did not personally eyewitness the action undertaken to liberate Malisevo from the KLA. Am I -- am I correct then in -- in coming to the conclusion that you -- I'm sorry. I understand there was a translation error in my question. I was talking about the operation to liberate Malisevo from the KLA, not the operation of the KLA to liberate Malisevo. I'm told the B/C/S had a minor tweak in that. Anyway, sir, the question I was posing for you is: Can we conclude that you did not personally eyewitness the commencement of any actions undertaken by the Serbian security forces during the time period that you were on the ground, and we're talking about commencement, the actual first strike, if you will?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said yesterday, sir, we -- we came back out of Malisevo to -- to be met at Kijevo, Lapusnik, and to see substantial VJ and MUP forces with tanks deployed, ready. And I think I spoke to I think the gentleman called Legija, that he was the commander of that particular element, and I cannot believe he was just sat on the side of the road, you know, waiting for a picnic. It was quite clear this was an assault force waiting to move into the Malisevo area.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, you mentioned the gentleman called Legija. Could you -- had you met him before? How did you know his identity? How did you recognise him?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I remember correctly, sir, he introduced himself to me and asked who I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: So I am duty-bound to tell him who I was and produced my licna karta to verify my identity and that of the French DA as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did he introduce himself as Legija, or did he give you a name?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: He just said Legija.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: All right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I am aware, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned Kijevo a few moments ago. I'd like to focus on Kijevo for a couple of questions, since I believe in your earlier testimony you had mentioned this area as one where you encountered some armed local defences from that village. And I think that you also said that the village was surrounded by Albanian villages and was of particular interest to the KLA. Can we conclude from that the fact that the KLA actually had Kijevo blockaded and attacked during the time period you are talking about?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: They -- they certainly were around the area, sir. Whether one could say it was a physical blockade, I would suggest that that blockade could be forced if the Serbian security forces had wished to do so, and there was must have been some kind of resupply in because this was quite an isolated area right in the middle of Kosovo itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, allow me to focus your attention specifically to June of 1998, to ask if you heard at that time or had information or knowledge of the fact that the village was besieged by four KLA positions that surrounded it such that some 1.400 villagers, the majority of whom were Albanian, the rest Serb and Roma, as well as a police detachment that was in that village were blockaded in the village for the better part of one month, with armed helicopters being utilised to air-drop food, munitions, and supplies, as well as to evacuate -- there were I believe two pregnant women and several wounded during the course of this blockade. Do you recall that particular incident, either hearing about it or witnesses any portion of it?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: During -- you said the month of June, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the month of June, as I say, I was back in the United Kingdom for our first, senior daughter's wedding. I understand there were some operations in that area, but I was not actually in province at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Fair enough.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I think what you say, I wouldn't disagree with. There were UCK positions around the area, and it had been and was a bone of contention throughout 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. Now, the -- probably either the last or the second to last area that I have questions about deal with my client. Now, am I correct that you never had or that you don't recall any specific contact with General Sreten Lukic of the MUP?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not as far as I'm aware, sir. I mentioned yesterday that there were the normal national days where senior gentlemen from the MUP were present. But as I mentioned that yesterday, it was a fairly stilted meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, then, perhaps you can help me clear up a matter of apparent confusion. In your June 2006 statement at paragraph 14, when talking about the Glodjane or Radonjic Lake incident where you visits the crime scene of the people alleged to have been killed by the KLA, at that time in that statement -- I take that back. At that time the statement says that you recalled that a lieutenant colonel from Djakovica was in charge of the crime site, possibly Sreten Lukic. Now, is it possible that you only knew the last name of the lieutenant colonel from Djakovica and that someone from the Office of the Prosecutor suggested to you the first name of General Sreten Lukic?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's a very interesting question. I don't believe it was General Sreten Lukic, no. I believe the rank on the person's uniform was -- was a lieutenant colonel, as I perceive. If there has been a misnaming of the person concerned, then that is not -- that is not intentional, no. I just believe the gentleman was Lieutenant Colonel Lukic. Whether there was a Sreten Lukic, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Now, when dealing with this Radonjic Lake incident, did you have occasion after the visit to the crime site to go to the Hotel Patrick in Djakovica where the autopsies were being performed on the bodies that were recovered from the crime scene?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't, sir, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said yesterday, we used to use the hotel as a base on a very open basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes. I do recall that from yesterday. Just one moment, sir. Let me just check one more thing. Well, Colonel, I thank you for your time. I have completed all my questions. Thank you very much for you cooperation and you were answers.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ivetic. Mr. Crosland, I have just one question at this stage. Could you look, please, at paragraph 44 of your statement, and bearing in mind the discussion we had about paragraph 50 and 51, can you tell me if there are inaccuracies in paragraph 44?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, they're not, sir. All we -- if I may. I took Lord Ashdown around a comprehensive visit all over Kosovo, so in order to -- for him to better understand as an envoy for the -- for the Prime Minister, I believe, the entire scene. So although we've concentrated here on saying about Prilep, Rznic, and Suva Reka, because those were some key areas at that particular time, he travelled fairly comprehensively throughout Kosovo, including going down to the Pagarusa valley with the head of the UNHCR at the time to view the IDP situation which is of grave concern.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But to be absolutely clear about this, you've told us, I think, that he visited on two occasions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And I believe you were assisted in your recollection of these as being September and December.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It was also my impression at that point that you were not necessarily with a BBC film crew although he was, but were you actually there along with the BBC film crew?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The BBC film crew, sir, came specifically with Lord Ashdown.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And you were there as well, though, while they were working with him.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We travelled in my -- my vehicle separately, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And the filming they did was on only one of these two visits; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We filmed -- I can recall very clearly the shell-fire incident from Blace onto Suva Reka villages to the west. We also went to Glodjane to see the site of the massacre that we have been discussing, sir. Whether the BBC came on both trips, I am afraid I can't recall, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And on one of these trips, there was a homemade video by one of your staff.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's right, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Ms. Carter, is any of this film available to the Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I began searching when this came up previously. I do not see that it's within our -- the MOS team individual exhibit list, but I have heard rumour that there is some sort of BBC footage within the Tribunal. I will continue searching for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You perhaps should review Ashdown's evidence in the Milosevic trial.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And it may also assist you to review the evidence of General Delic in the Milosevic trial.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: I will make that undertaking, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We note that we also have power to call for evidence if -- if we consider identified evidence may assist us in determining the issues in the trial.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Respectfully, Your Honour, our amazing case manager has yet again found an item for us. Apparently, V000-3823 is indicating that it is Lord Paddy Ashdown visit to Kosovo, 1998, BBC news footage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But does that have an exhibit number in this trial?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Do you have questions in re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The Court has already covered one topic, thus I have only two remaining.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Colonel Crosland, yesterday, you were shown a document entitled, 4D137, and I'd like to bring that onto the screen. This document, if I were -- is it on your screen?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not yet, ma'am, no. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Colonel, yesterday, you were examined by Mr. Ackerman in regards to this document, and the implication was that General Perisic, while telling you one thing, was writing orders saying something different. If I were to hold out to you that this item, rather than being an immediate order, is a document pertaining to a war plan about how something would develop. It is not an executive order to be implemented right away, that the decision to implement such a plan could not come for the General Staff and the Chief of the General Staff bypassing an institution superior to him; that instead to enact an order such as this, the president of the state and the Supreme Defence Council would have to approve. If I were to hold out to you, again, that this was a plan to be implemented -- a contingency plan to be implemented at a later date, do you believe that Perisic was talking out of both sides of his mouth, to use the phrase?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Forgive me for being a simple soldier. This document - and I apologise sincerely if I'm not answering the question - to me, this document gives firsthand evidence of the chain of command and is exactly what I would have expected to have been produced as a directive prior to an operational order which I think is in one of the annexes, if I remember rightly, by General Samardzic, the commander of the 3rd Army then to be passed down to General -- General Pavkovic, who was then 52 Corps commander in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, ma'am, if I may just say. The interesting thing is that we discussed endlessly, yesterday, why the VJ General Staff were very diffident about saying that there were joint operations, and this document here quite clearly says that the VJ will act in concert with the MUP, which is entirely feasible and understandable. But it took an awfully long time, in fact up till August when General Ojdanic gave the briefing, that it was admitted that there were joint operations.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Do you -- as a professional soldier, would it be reasonable for contingency plans to be made for use in the future?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: This, ma'am, is standard -- is standard practice. Obviously, the more contingency plans one has hopefully the better the operations will be carried out with less casualties on both sides. There are situations when you have to react very quickly, and the commanders, the field commanders, may have to make decisions in the best interests of their troops at the time. Whether those are the correct decisions is very easy to make in hindsight.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ms. Carter, we're alert to the issue that is focused by this document and the way in which evidence of General Vasiljevic touched upon it. But can I ask you if you're then going to deal with 4D140.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Yes, that is the next document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You're going ask questions of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Colonel Crosland, I'd now like to direct your attention to 4D140, which you intimated in your previous answer, which is an order that would be issued by the 3rd Army command in conjunction with this directive. I would like to point you to page 6 of this document, specifically to the bottom of the page at 5.1. Colonel, in this document it indicates that in the first phase of this engagement, six lines down, that the 37th Motorised Brigade of the 2nd Army would be engaged within this plan. Sir, you indicated, in paragraph 69 of your statement, that you saw a brigade that was at issue shortly before you left Kosovo, that a brigade had entered into Raska at that time. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, ma'am, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please understand that Raska is -- is north of the province of Kosovo and, therefore, not involved in the actual territorial area.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: So it would make sense that the 37th Motorised Brigade would be noted as a 2nd Army brigade?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct from the -- from the order of battle, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Okay. And would you, again, anticipate that an order of battle would also be drawn up so in the event that a triggering event occurs then all orders can proceed immediately?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That would be reasonable contingency planning, ma'am, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: And you don't object to the drawing up of these plans or think that it's somehow different than normal operating procedure of a military installation; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not quite certain, with respect, ma'am, where you're coming from. And forgive me, I've forgotten of date of this particular -- this is the initial --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's the day after the one that you just look at a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: It would be the end of July, 1998.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: This then would be then in preparation, as I made clear in my report, that the Serbian security offensive started in late August which would be in time for this order to be carried out.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: May I bring up P number 2166, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What is that document? Please don't do that just immediately, because I may have more questions on this one. What is P2166?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: P2166 is the minutes of the meeting of the operations of the interdepartmental staff. What I'm attempting to point out that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Don't tell me any more about that, but that question is related to the interpretation of these two documents, is it, or is it a separate issue you're moving on to?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: No. It's interpretation of these two documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. You may carry on.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Looking to P2166, on page 3, four paragraphs from the bottom. Colonel, in this document, it says, "Pursuant to the decision adopted at the 5th session of the Supreme Defence Council on 9 June 1998, the law on the Yugoslav Army, the Defence Law, and the Rules of Service of the Yugoslav Army, a plan to suppress terrorism in Kosovo and Metohija was drawn up which provided for the engagement of units of the Serbian MUP and the Yugoslav Army." Would you agree with me that at the time of this contingency plan being drawn up, there was already a plan in place and active based on the -- I'm sorry, based on the operation interdepartmental staff minutes?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: That appears to be correct, ma'am, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, again, to follow up on this point, I would like show you P940. These are collegium minutes of 21 February, 1999. Looking to page 4, to the middle of the page, beginning with the paragraph that starts "Pursuant to our decisions," in the middle of the page. This -- these collegium minutes were held on 21 February, 1999. They indicate that, "Pursuant to our decisions, the 37th Motorised Brigade from Raska was preparing for the carrying out of tasks according to the plan of the 3rd Army commander for attachment to the Pristina Corps command." Given that the original directive and order, which you had been viewing with Ackerman, indicates that the 37th Motorised Brigade would be activated upon that order, would you agree that it appears that the order becomes active somewhere near 21 February, 1999, where the 37th Motorised Brigade is brought into Raska -- or brought from Raska?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: That -- that appears to be the case, ma'am, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: And is this also consistent with your paragraph 69 where you indicate seeing another brigade at Raska?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: That -- that appears, as I made clear, that we had found these extra brigades at a time when the KDOM force was under considerable problems with the Ambassador Walker I think had been PNG'd, and so their time on the ground was very limited, and to see a further three brigades joining the force was of concern, as I made clear to the Court yesterday, ma'am, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: And, temporally, given that the collegium minutes speaking about this activation were on 21 February, 1999, that is also consistent with the time in which you saw this extra brigade at Raska; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would be within the time frame, ma'am, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Now, you said that it was of concern to bring in these three extra brigades based on the firepower that was already available within Kosovo and Metohija; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did -- I made that statement, ma'am, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Okay. I would now like to bring up P2591.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Still on the same subject?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: That is the command of the 37th Motorised Brigade, and it is dated 23 April, 1999. I would like to direct you to page 2 of that document, specifically the fourth bullet. Colonel Crosland, in the order -- or the command from the 37th Motorised Brigade, the writer notes that,"Engagement of relatively large forces to fight small terrorist groups using an elephant to kill a fly. Instead of less trained forces for sealing off the area and then sending specially able bodied and well-equipped forces to destroy a terrorist within a closed space, it would have been more effective if a series of low intensity and undoubtedly successful actions were carried out, instead of --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please slow down when reading.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: -- mopping up operations just to take a walk through the area." Colonel Crosland, do you agree with the assessment the 37th Motorised Brigade based on what you saw in Kosovo and Metohija through 1998 and through the time that you were there in 1999 at the run-up of the NATO bombing?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am. It's been put far more eloquently than I could have put it. I'm not a staff officer. I'm an operational officer, and that's what I've been saying all the way along at that there were huge and disproportionate forces required to carry out -- they never really, in my opinion, got to grips with a counter-terrorist or counter-insurgency operation, and this paragraph sums it up very eloquently.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel Crosland. That's the last question I have on this topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Could you had he me then by explaining how this demonstrates bypassing the normal chain of command which was the area explored in cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Respectfully, Your Honour. What was explored on cross-examination based on Mr. Ackerman's questioning was how Perisic could on one hand be indicating to him that he has taken issue with the VJ being engaged within the interior of Kosovo while the same handwriting this order. That is what I was trying to clarify, that there was already an order in place, that Perisic was not doing what was being held out by Mr. Ackerman; and then following through that you can see when the engagement occurs, because that unit comes in according to the minutes of the supreme -- I'm sorry, of the General Staff sometime in February, which is consistent with what Colonel Crosland saw on the ground.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. But the thing I'm really interested in is the evidence if it exists of bypassing the normal chain of command, which is the point that Perisic and his colleague made to Colonel Crosland. He left him certainly with the impression that they considered that that was occurring and that there was a direct route from Milosevic to Pavkovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, where is the tangible evidence of that?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I thought it was supposed to exist in some of this documentation, but you concede it's not in this documentation.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think one can look to -- to the P2166. I'm not sure if you want me to point this out, especially in front of the witness. But even then Colonel Pavkovic is the primary speaker about what is occurring at this time, that he is appearing to take a primary role as opposed to merely the Pristina Corps lieutenant general, as what is noted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, that's a matter that will no doubt be explored later. I just wanted to be sure there was nothing else to be drawn through examination of the witness from these documents. So please carry on with the other issues you have to deal with in re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time we would seek to admit P2591 as well as P940.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Colonel Crosland, the last topic that I would like to address with you came up yesterday in your cross-examination with regards to the situation reports and diplomatic telegrams, which were produced by you and by Ambassador Donnelly while on the ground. Can you please explain to the Court what each of these items are, and how you are related to the drafting of each.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: The -- the diplomatic telegrams would be initiated by the ambassador or his deputy, the Deputy Head of Mission, and that states quite clearly on the top of the telegram that it is a diplomatic telegram. Within the diplomatic telegram, the DipTel for short, content of any interests of a military nature would be drafted by myself for inclusion in the -- in the ambassador's telegram. And he, of course, would check to see that I hadn't overstepped the mark in any of my observations. So that is the diplomatic telegram procedure which during 1998 I believe over a thousand were sent. The other telegrams which were initiated as BritMil Belgrade would be drafted and initialed by myself or one of the members of my staff if I was away. They would out of courtesy be reviewed by either the Deputy Head of Mission or the ambassador, because one was working as part of his team as part British embassy in Belgrade. And I was also accredited to the Vojska Jugoslavija and, therefore, had to make certain the comments were appropriate to my position as defence attache.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: So in the Court reviewing each of these documents, the situation reports, they can take as your direct comment on the situation on the ground; and as to the diplomatic telegrams, anything that is making reference to the military aspects, that would be from your assessment as well; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: In essence, that is entirely correct, ma'am. The slightly muddling factor is that because I was down in Kosovo on a very permanent basis, there were comments passed by satellite phone both back to Belgrade and back to -- to London which were of an immediate nature. And, therefore, they may not be properly recorded, but may well have been added to the diplomatic telegrams that went out, as I say, on a very regular basis as the situation became more critical.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The situation reports that were just referred to, were they submitted unrevised by ambassador or deputy.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would say most of the time, Your Honour, they would always be looked at by one or other, either the deputy or the ambassador or the first political officer, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do they run in your name, though?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They would go out as a military telegram, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Your Honour, that completes the two topics in which I had to address with the witness during redirect examination, and I just thank the witness for his time and his service to the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Colonel, I have a question for you, please.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: You've given us an impression and that's what I understand, that the KLA was something not that huge. It was puny. And the forces that were on the opposite side consisting of VJ and MUP, they were big and colossal and, therefore, was too much force used against the little force in the beginning, which of course grew up and became more organised in later on. What would have been the fate of things if MUP and VJ had not applied so much of force, in your estimation, please? Would the fate of things been different to what there emerged today or what as we see them in tangible shape today? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I think the main bone of contention that I have with the actions carried out by the Vojska Jugoslavija and the MUP were, in my opinion, not the correct actions to try and isolate and then -- we will call it fix, fix and find. Now, I don't believe that during the entire 1998, 1999 scenario, the KLA were either properly fixed or properly found. Now, that is a question of tactics. In the experience that I've had in dealing with several counter-insurgency operation, this is a long-term procedure, sir. Several that I've been involved in have taken between six and 12 years to come to a successful conclusion. Now, success depends on which side of the boundary you are. So there was an attempt to try, if I may use a rather drastic analogy, to blast the UK -- or UCK, rather, or KLA out of the territory, which inevitably led to, as I've said many, many times, huge destruction and, and I was told also this, ethnic cleansing. But I think if your house is blown out and you're forced out of it running at gunpoint, I would suggest that is actually a fairly frightening and devastating experience, and I think inevitably - and I did indicate this to the General Staff in the meetings that I had - that this problem was not an easily solvable problem, bearing in mind that we had a completely porous border on the Albanian side through which copious men and materiel, funding, everything that is required for an insurgency operation was extremely difficult if not impossible to stop. So as the insurgency went on and as we have indicated, perhaps the opinion of the international community started to, if I may be so bold - and it's a personal opinion - to get behind this fledgling organisation for whatever reason, this gave heart at a time when it -- certainly in the late autumn, the KLA did suffer pretty severe losses and were pushed back by the MUP and the VJ. We then had the intervention of the ACTORD in October, I think it is, which the VJ and the MUP, as I indicated yesterday, sir, withdrew in good order as -- as ordered. And directly back into that, into the vacuum that was created by them moving back, in came the KLA; and I witnessed that virtually in each combat location that the VJ had just departed from. So you could say that the Vojska Jugoslavija and the MUP forces were probably on a no win situation. Now, that may be being certainly controversial. It may be -- and I don't wish -- and it may also be minimalising the problem. The point I'm trying to make to you, sir, is that a counter-insurgency operation requires good intelligence. It requires a good degree of patience. It requires a hearts and minds policy to win round people. And, as I indicated, the majority of the villagers in the early days really did not want a fertile area like Kosovo to become a battle ground, which unfortunately it did throughout the summer and August and late autumn of 1998 and 1999. So I would make my comment that I believe the wrong type of tactics, albeit in the Balkans, unfortunately we have seen a series of hard actions fought at a long range. It does require soldiers to -- to do patrolling, to occupy the ground, and to dominate the area so that you actually have the intelligence. Again, this is a difficult situation. I mean, it's not unlike when our forces in Northern Ireland, where we were the goldfish in the bowl. And to get intelligence from another nation or another -- another language is extremely difficult. So it is not -- there is no easy quick fix way, and I think the idea of blasting the -- the KLA out of the area, in my opinion, has led to more problems than there are already and currently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think appropriately Ms. Carter raised some matters with regard to Exhibit P2166 that -- that actually were new matter, and I would like to ask maybe two or three questions taking less than five minutes, if I could be permitted to do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Respectfully, Your Honour, this P2166 was actually used quite extensively in my original examination. I did follow up with regards to the 37th Motorised Brigade. However, I do not believe that I have opened any new issues that were not available to Mr. Ackerman as it was extensively discussed during direct examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I don't agree with that, but -- okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You're not prepared to accept his professional judgement of the matter that might assist us, bearing in mind that you will get any opportunity that's necessary to come back? Is it really helping the process to obstruct that?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Respectfully, Your Honour, if the Prosecution is again allowed to follow up, then, no, I do not. I just believe that he was taking a second bite at the apple.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ackerman please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Can we get P2166 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Colonel, while that's coming up, I think probably the first thing you'll agree with me about is -- is looking at isolated documents without having access to the whole of communications that were going on is sometimes risky in terms of determining what was really happening. That's true, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possibly not the right -- the right way of doing things, sir, but we'll try and pull things together.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If you'll look at the first page of this document, right at the very last paragraph -- well, first I want you to notice up in the list of persons present that one of the persons present there was General Perisic and another was General Aleksandar Dimitrijevic. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Then in the last paragraph, you'll see that Lieutenant General Nebojsa Pavkovic gave a brief report on the implementation of the plan. Now, this is in November of 1998 after the directive of Perisic in July and after the order of Samardzic following up that directive. In November, General Pavkovic is giving a brief report on the implementation of the plan for suppressing terrorism. If we go then to page 2, you will see in the first paragraph that he talks about a plan that was carried out in stages over a period of 45 to 55 days.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And then if you go to the very -- next to the last page, where there is a series of conclusions.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't yet got that page, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. It will be up in a minute.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: We're at the bottom of page -- I think it's 15?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, it sounds as though this is all material that you would be perfectly capable of making submissions about without simply the witness by the nose through words of the document. The document is now available to us for consideration and interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I actually considered that, Your Honour. You may be right. I think -- I think I agree with you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do you want to ask anything further, Ms. Carter?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. There are one or two outstanding issues about documents and, indeed, the statement itself. Parties have addressed these, I think, adequately. We will make a determination about the outstanding issues and either issue it in writing early next week or state it orally when we next sit, but the position will be clarified by the time we are hearing not the next witness but the one after that. That completes your evidence, Mr. Crosland. Thank you for coming again to the Tribunal to give evidence. I can't say that you're free forever of that responsibility, bearing in mind the other matters in which you are involved.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But for the moment you're free to leave. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We need to go into closed session for that.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: First, as to Exhibit P00683, that is either a situation report or diplomatic telegram. Either way, it was received from the United Kingdom. It appears that the document that we uploaded into e-court actually is the unredacted version of that, and thus the unredacted version needs to be taken under seal. A redacted version will be substituted for the public display striking the receipt -- the receipt list. As to the second issue, it appears Ms. Grogan, again, has located the video that the Court wishes to take under consideration, and that is P00611. The videos are not in e-court. However, copies can be provided to the Court, hard copies specifically can certainly be provided to the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's actually now a great pity that the witness has just been released, is it not, when this is an exhibit in the case. We might have been assisted in his evidence on something that I think we are left rather confused about. Is that video available to show just now?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: It appears it would take a few moments, Your Honour. Your Honour, it would certainly be available after the break, if the Court choose to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The trouble is the witness has a commitment, and I'm inclined to ask him to come back and view it and tell us where it was taken and what's in it, because we can't make an assessment of a video on its own. The trouble is that he has a commitment, and we're doing our best to make sure that he could meet it. I think the thing to do would be for us to adjourn just now and for the witness to be allowed to view the video and then for me to ask him a number of questions in relation to it. And if arising out of that there are questions the parties which to ask, then you would have an opportunity of doing that. But if there is something in there that could assist us, then we would be in dereliction of our responsibilities if we didn't do it when a witness like this is available to us.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Your Honour, my only comment would be to be open with the Court. When the Colonel left, the intern left with him to say goodbye, so there has been communication between the Prosecution and the witness. So I just want to make an effort of transparency.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. We'll try to intercept him. There is one matter we can deal with. We will probably still can finish before the break and the break will be available for him, and we'll cut it short if necessary -- well, no, we won't. But we'll make sure he leaves on time for his commitment. The Prosecution have made an application for an adjournment of a week. It may be there's no opposition to that. I don't know. I see no one leaping to their feet. But we're not immediately inclined to grant that application, because if K54 is to give evidence and that matter has yet to be resolved, that evidence could be taken at the end of next week. It could be taken on Thursday and Friday. And bearing in mind the developments that indicate the Prosecution case may be concluded in the month of March, we now need to address the issue of the presentation of the Defence case, and we don't want to address that issue without giving the parties an opportunity to comment on how they see the position, before we start making orders. We had in mind to make an order fairly soon, and this has obviously brought the issue to a head. So we also have in mind that we could use Wednesday to discuss how we proceed, and we would make our decision pretty quickly after that on the future of the case. We also hand in mind, and you should have this in your minds when you're considering what submissions to make, we had in mind to have a recess during the first two weeks of April, and that may well fit neatly into the progress of the case now. But you should factor that into any consideration you're making of the appropriate further procedure. We do not think written filings are necessary on this. We think we would consider Wednesday to be a Status Conference. Now, does anyone take issue with that suggested procedure which would leave Monday and Tuesday free so far as you're concerned, but it would enable us also on Monday and Tuesday to deal with one or two outstanding issues and give you decisions on them later next week, too. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, the only observation I'd make is that there's a contingency with regard to Witness K54, and I understand reserving Thursday and Friday for K54 is appropriate; however, if this decision that K54 is not to be called, then perhaps the Status Conference can be on Friday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think that's a reasonable proposition, so we can be flexible in the arrangements we make. Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, as you can see, we all abided by your request to be efficient. What we have at hand here is that it seems that the part of that week will be lost, and we hear now that we'll probably have to start with our case in April. It is a waste of time for me to sit here and wait for Wednesday to see whether I'd be working on Thursday and Friday. Therefore, I wanted to support what Mr. Ackerman had said. When we have a full week off, we can go to Belgrade. Our witnesses are there. I also have to say that it's not only a problem for Mr. Hannis to chase the witnesses around. This is an issue for us as well, of witnesses refusing to appear. I do not object to his principle of working because I understand I'll be in the same position and I'll be handed red and yellow cards by you as well. That is the problem. I'm sorry, but that's the way it is. Truth may not cannot be pleasant. We would prefer to have a full week off to do be able to leave and do down there; otherwise, what am I to do in The Hague to wait for Wednesday to whether until we'll have the witness on Thursday and Friday? Perhaps your decision -- decision will have to be against that, so as not to waste the entire week. Perhaps I can ask for your indulgence in that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Can I speak with the interpreters, please. I know it's important to have this break at a quarter to 11.00 for half an hour. But I wonder if in the exceptional circumstances it might be possible to continue, to view this video which takes only four minutes, and for me then to ask some questions and allow any further questions that arise, and then to have the break and, if necessary, a longer break. But it would enable us to complete the witness and allow him still to make his connection.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: That is fine with the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We can do that. Will you bring the witness back in, please. We'll go into closed session for that purpose.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I apologise for the confusion, Mr. Crosland. But in the rush at the end, it came to our attention as soon as you had left that there is available, apparently, part of a BBC video, which has the number P -- is it 166, did you say?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: 611, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: 611. So that is now going to be played on your screen. If you just watch it in silence with the rest of us, I will ask you some questions once it's completed. There's no reason why this can't be broadcast, is there? THE PROSECUTOR: No, Your Honour. It was broadcast on the BBC.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: "[Inaudible] unquestionably an act of criminality for which I have absolutely no doubt individuals in command and the politicians who have allowed it on the Serb side could be indicted as war criminals.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: "When? Which villages? "[Inaudible] "You mean up here, up in the mountains? "These mountains here. "And what happened? When did they [inaudible]. "[Inaudible] "Shoot with what, with guns or -- [inaudible]. Mortars. "Machine-guns also. "How long have they been travel? "About five days "What is happening now? Where are they going -- where are they going now? "[Inaudible] The mountains. "Are -- they're telling us this village is under attack next; right? "Until 12.00 they have a deadline [inaudible] "But are they going to now, further on up? "In the mountains. She said -- she told me that [inaudible]. "[Inaudible] "Five months."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We make it clear at the outset that we will have no regard at all to the comments made by Ashdown in the first segment, and we shall not have regard to the conversation in the second section because it's so unclear and, of course, the first section was simply an assertion of an opinion about which we're not able to explore the basis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The way you can help us, Mr. Crosland, is this: There are two episodes there; one showing Lord Ashdown viewing open countryside, and the second one showing him meeting people who bear the appearance of refugees. Did both of these occur on the one visit?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Recalled]
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The first video clip of Lord Ashdown was with my binoculars, and that was overlooking the position of Suva Reka at a distance towards -- we were to the west of Suva Reka on the high ground in the area of a village called Studencani. And I was -- had drawn his attention to the fact that artillery fire was coming from the battle group area of -- in the area of Dulje, which is just north of Suva Reka, which was a recognised Vojska Jugoslavija battle group position. And it was directed into the area, and I repeat the area, because I don't have a detailed map here, of the village of Budakovo. And it was quite clear that, as I made clear to Lord Ashdown, you could hear the guns firing, the crump, the shells landing, and then the blast of the shells being fired, what in the military we call crack and thump. And he accepted, and being ex-military himself, that that was a correct assertion by me that artillery was firing into the area of this village, and you could see the houses that were then subsequently alight.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: At one point, there seemed to be quite a widespread area of smoke rising. Was that all the result of action against one village?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Recalled]
utterances.text: If I remember rightly, Your Honour, that was the action of artillery fire against a number of villages to the north and east of Suva Reka.
