There were -- Budakovo was one of the main ones, and there were several smaller hamlets in that area which were also receiving attention. The second part of that video, if I remember rightly, was on the same day. We arranged for Lord Ashdown to meet with Mary Morgan, the head of the UNHCR, to do a private visit to the area of the Pagarusa valley, where there were about 40.000 IDPs. Now, whether that was in the Pagarusa valley or whether that was at another site, because there were various -- you will appreciate, sir, that these scenes were fairly widespread throughout the area. The Pagarusa visit, I left Lord Ashdown to do the visit entirely by himself so that there was no pressure from my vehicle as the defence attache's vehicle being in that particular part of his programme. So I can't say which -- where exactly that footage was shot. But as I said, it was an all too familiar performance throughout Kosovo during the summer of 1998, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And can you remember whether that was the September or the December visit? Does the weather and the state of the countryside help?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Recalled]
utterances.text: I am afraid I can't say with any certainty, sir, no. I will have to relook at my statement, sir. I apologise for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You referred to villages from which the smoke was coming, being to the north and east of Suva Reka. You also mentioned that at one stage in your evidence, just now, something occurring to the west of Suva Reka on high ground in the area of Studencani. Could you clarify that for me, please.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Recalled]
utterances.text: On this particular visit, there was heavy MUP and VJ presence in the town of Suva Reka, which was really the -- the frontier between that particular position and then Dulje, Blace, where the battle group was; so in between was, if you will, KLA territory. And in order to try and get Lord Ashdown in as close as possible, we carried out a cross-country route into the area; otherwise, having driven straight up the main road to Suva Reka, we would have been stopped by a MUP check-point. So to get the best vantage point, I decided to take a cross-country route up into the area of Studencani which overlooked this troubled area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So that was your location, west of Suva Reka and toward Studencani?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Recalled]
utterances.text: Yes. And that is where that initial shot of Paddy Ashdown's forearm with my binoculars was taken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, does any Defence counsel wish to explore anything in relation to the video? No. Ms. Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, that does now complete your evidence. Thank you for coming back and assisting us further. We'll go into closed session so you can leave. And we will now adjourn and resume at quarter to 12.00.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, one question you could perhaps assist us with. Assuming all the witnesses that you intend to lead do actually give evidence, and assuming that there was no evidence led next week, when do you say the Prosecution evidence will be completed?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think we would finish by the second -- or third week in March. Maybe the week of the -- I'm trying to think what that Monday is. The 19th, that week in March.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do you also have a rough estimate of how long the evidence of this next witness will take today?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: This witness today?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: An hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ms. Dragulev?

utterances.speaker: MS. DRAGULEV
utterances.text: Your Honour, direct examination won't be longer than 30 minutes, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That would suggest that we can return to the issue of next week at the end of the witness's evidence and use what time we have at that stage, perhaps even to explore one or two other time tabling issues. So we'll proceed now with the evidence of the witness K20, and for that we need to go into closed session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, who would like to initiate the debate on the time scale and time lines for the period after the close of the Prosecution evidence? Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, we did meet and discuss over the lunch break; and given the fact we had ten or 12 lawyers together discussing the same issues, I think you'll and amazed at the consensus that we've come to in some regards. We say that there are two -- I believe you want to discuss two areas. One is the remainder of the Prosecutor's case and the schedule, thereafter. Our request is that we use this session now for us to speak in turn on some of these points. I'll give you a broad overview of where we stand right now. I think you may see that we would -- we may end up at the end of this session in the position where we'd like to supplement in writing perhaps, to amplify and to show the Chamber why we've taken -- or are taking the positions we are taking. But for now let's just proceed looking at these two areas. For the remainder of the case, we, first of all, support the Prosecutor's motion to adjourn next week. If we look at the proposed witnesses that are scheduled, some of whom have not been decided upon, we see they are very important witnesses. They're big witnesses, including experts. We continue to receive a vast amount of disclosure in relation to many of these witnesses. We just received more CDs again this morning. Time is needed for us for the remainder of this case to be in a position to be effective. So we support the adjournment, and we await Your Honours' decision on the outstanding issues regarding whether or not the contested witnesses can come. So that's all we have to say about that period, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And do you see the 23rd of March as realistic assessment of when the evidence may conclude?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Well, we have no reason to doubt that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, to that extent, it's in your hands. The Prosecution set the timing, but we've been fairly flexible depending on how much you need to spend with witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Well, this is probably an area where we haven't had a chance to properly consider that, Your Honour, whether or not that's realistic. As for the matters following the close of the Prosecutor's case, there is of course the timing of two events. That's the 98 bis submissions, your decision on 98 bis, and of course the commencement of Defence cases or perhaps more correctly the filing of our 65 ter submissions following your judgement under Rule 98 bis. Broadly speaking, our position on 98 bis, the Rule provides for oral submissions by the parties, followed by an oral decision by the Chamber. We feel we can be in a position to argue that at the end of that second week in April, after the week -- after the two-week break in April. We will request that we can file written submissions in support of those oral submissions. The Rule does not preclude that. We're thinking of perhaps an aide-memoire or some sort of a skeleton of argument that would assist the Chamber. Following that, your decision will come down under Rule 98 bis. And, thereafter, the time frame we think is reasonable given all the circumstances, and my colleagues will speak more specifically on their individual situations. We feel that a four-month period after the judgement of 98 bis would be reasonable for us to file our 65 ter submission. Those are the broad strokes of -- and the results of our discussion. My colleagues do have specific points they want to raise in relation to some of these matters, and I believe Mr. Ackerman would like to speak first to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You don't want to take the matter any further and give any indication of the sort of time you envisage for the Defence case or cases?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: That really is premature, and I think by the end of the hearing you'll hear what the position of the six Defence teams is. You may get a better flavour for that. I'm not in a position to convey that to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I, of course, associate myself with the remarks of Mr. O'Sullivan, and I'll just amplify maybe very briefly. As to the question you asked Mr. O'Sullivan about do we think that the Prosecutor's estimate of the second or third week of March is realistic, I think it probably is. I think Mr. Hannis made that estimate based on his experience with the length of cross-examination we've done with regard to some of these more difficult witnesses, and I suspect that he has considered that carefully enough that he believes that's a pretty realistic number. It may depend on some outstanding motions regarding certain witnesses there. A witness like General Clark, for instance, is obviously not going to be a one-day witness. He would be here for some time, I would think, if he comes. And so that can certainly affect that ending time. But if we assume that that's correct, and it may very well be and in many ways I hope it is; then it seems that the suggestion that the 98 bis arguments take place after that April recess makes a lot of sense, because we would have that time then to fine tune those and make them as cogent as we possibly can. When we get beyond that, things get a little more dicey, and there is not a lot of an ability right now among the Defence teams, as I understand it, to make very good estimates and I'll explain that to you, I think. Your Honours recall that especially for the three newer accused that we were all taking the position rather loudly and vociferously back last spring that we certainly were not prepared to start trial in July when we in fact started trial. And I think Your Honours have probably observed in the occasionally disjointed nature of my cross-examination, at least, that I've been learning this case as I've gone along, and that has -- we've gone at a rate, and I think a rate that -- that with it was a lot of cooperation from -- from the Defence to try to help you get to the position where we've kind of got to now. I think we've been very cooperative in terms of things like that, and we have -- we've not asked, as Your Honour has suggested we could on a number of occasions, for additional time to prepare cross-examination for certain witnesses if we really were not able to be prepared. That's happened almost never. I think maybe once or twice it's happened, but rarely. And so I think we have been quite cooperative in getting to this point. But we paid a price for doing that, and the price we paid for doing that was we didn't have any time to be preparing the Defence case. And just to give you an example of how that plays out, right now I have a very long witness list, and I can't imagine that I would want to call anywhere near the number of people that are on that witness list. But until I can actually go to Serbia and talk to those witnesses and get some idea of -- of why they're on the list and what it is they're to be called for and what use they can be to my defence, I can't make a judgement about that. My guess is given a descent amount of time to do, that a witness list that might 40 people on it now, would wind up with somewhere between five and ten, and a presentation time that might be six weeks, would wind up being a week or two. So I think there's a lot to be gained from allowing a significant preparation time between the close of the Prosecution's case and the beginning of the Defence case. The -- the problem, of course, is we don't know who the rest of the witnesses are going to be for sure, and we don't know exactly how their witnesses are going to turn out. You just take the last witness, Crosland. Before he came here, we had one opinion about how his evidence would play out, and now that he's finished we have a completely different view of how his evidence plays out, and that's going to be true I think of witnesses that continue to come, and that impacts what we might want to do in the Defence cases. What I'm hoping, and I think all the rest of us, too, is that we can with a significant amount of work tend to minimise the amount of time that we'll take to put on the Defence case and streamline it as much as possible, and I know it may sound at first blush to you that a request for a 120-day period in which to do that seems excessive and ridiculous. When you really look at the amount of work that has to be done to try to streamline this and make it work, it's probably not all that out of line. So that would be my suggestions to you at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You can't assist either on how long you envisage the presentation of Defence cases, bearing in mind that it has to bear a proportionate relationship to the Prosecution case if you feel the need to lead a significant number of witnesses. You can't help us in principle on how we might look at that issue also.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think I did try to do that. I think what I suggested that if I have enough time to do it, but I can take a list that right now is 40 and turn into five or ten. If it turns into five or ten, then I'm looking at a week or two. I can't speak for the rest of my colleagues. I don't know how much time my other colleagues are going to want to take. But I would be fully comfortable putting on a two-week defence if it's at all realistic, and I think that it might be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You see, that's an important factor in looking globally at the length of this trial, and that may well affect our approach to what on the face of it looks like a demand for an awful long time, certainly much more than I ever envisaged between cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I can only tell you this: Based on almost nothing but hunch, any time someone asked me where when case is going to be over, I say it's going to be over by the winter break this year. And I still think that's true and probably will beat that by quite a bit. That's what I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Who else wishes to address us from the Defence? Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would like to join the words of my colleagues Mr. O'Sullivan and Mr. Ackerman, and I would like to try and provide you with some more elements that we have taken into account at the present situation. During the Prosecution case, we have all witnessed very frequent situations when Prosecution witnesses' statements are changed at the last moment, and their viva voce testimony in the courtroom to a certain extent differs from what was provided to us in the Prosecution's submissions with regard to Rule 65 ter. From the point of view of my team, we interviewed some of the witnesses in 2002 and 2003. I would like to avoid the situation that the Prosecution has found themselves in; and that is because of the lapse of time between the interviews and the testimony of these witnesses, I'm not able to prepare them enough or at least to bring their testimony in such shape that will allow me for a very brief examination-in-chief according to Rule 94 ter and the other tools at my disposal that will enable me to curtail their testimony in chief as much as possible. On the other hand, I would like to say that we are still to hear some very important Prosecution witnesses which might call for a dozen new Defence witnesses, and I still don't know what these Prosecution witnesses are going to say in the courtroom. And I believe that it is premature for me to give you any serious forecast as to what will happen or instruct my investigators which witnesses to prepare. I'm going to mention just two witnesses that I am quite concerned about when it comes to the length of the Defence case. Those are Philip Coo and Witness who will talk about the justice system, the judiciary. Let me not mention his name. These two witnesses can either broaden or narrow down our list of witnesses, and they can also either broaden or narrow down the list of documents we're going to use in the courtroom. Since I have started talking about documents, I would like to draw your attention to the fact that unlike the Prosecution, we are in a somewhat less favourable situation in our preparations because we will probably be expected to provide all the documents in English at a certain point in time when the Chamber so decides, and I don't think that this will be technically feasible, at least to a large extent. And now we are in a situation that the Prosecution did not have. They would introduce documents, and their translations would follow much later. For example, yesterday, we received documents for blue book translated into Serbian; and should the situation be the other way round, if we are in the same situation, we will not be able to introduce a Serbian document. And we believe that this is a situation that is our weakness, bearing in mind that most of the documents that we're going to present will be in Serbian. I have already asked for some translations. I will continue doing that. But since I am still not aware of what I might need because the Prosecution witnesses have still not appeared, I still don't know how far should I go in requesting translation of documents. I believe that the time my colleague's Mr. Ackerman and Mr. O'Sullivan have asked for will help us curtail the time spent in the courtroom to a large extent, given the degree of preparations that we will have the time to do during that break. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Visnjic. Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, Your Honour, I would like to join the words of my predecessors. I would also like to say something on my part, on my behalf, as I spoke earlier today when I suggested that we shouldn't work next. I don't know if I heard it well when you said that the Trial Chamber is entitled to calling their own witnesses, and I was very happy to hear that. Article 98 of the Rules gives the Trial Chamber proprio motu, the right to call witnesses. If you should apply that Rule, as we do in our system of justice, then we will be able to curtail the proceedings to a large extent. For example, Mr. Crosland, today's witness. He has been referring the sources of two generals who said this or that or the other. If we take it into account that General Perisic is one of the accused, the other one is not accused but nobody's calling him. Then you have given a limited time to witness Stanic [as interpreted], who also gave us a hearsay evidence from the fourth-hand, coming from Stanisic to Milosevic. And all of these people, save for Milosevic, are alive and well. I am apologising for taking your time, and I am talking on my own behalf.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: This is helpful, but the witness you referred to there is recorded in the transcript as "Stanic." It was Tadic, was it? Tanic.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Tanic. Tanic is the name. When Jovica Milosevic fell, there was a new component. Rade Markovic, Zoran Mijatovic, and some others, Radonjic, and so on and so forth, and the name of the third person who was mentioned in a closed session. So we're talking about six more people for us to see whether Tanic really informed the general public that there would be shelling, whether he said it on TV. If there was death penalty, I would ask for a death penalty for that person who learned about that and did not warn the wretched people who were not alarmed. I would also like to remind you of a certain document issued by the Joint Command. There are several documents which are in dispute or not. If the Trial Chamber were to inspect those documents, you will see that there are at least 15 names in those documents. It arises from a statement from -- that we received from the Prosecution that a certain person authored those documents. Out of these 15 people, none were called to this Tribunal. These documents are introduced to other people who don't know anything about those documents, such as General Vasiljevic. What I'm trying to say here is if the Trial Chamber takes an effort and look at the number of witnesses who -- who provided hearsay evidence of something that they heard -- heard from people who are still alive, I know that Serbia cannot deliver General Mladic and others, but there are some other people who are not bound by the secrecy, by the confidentiality. They could be called. And if they come here, if they are called by the Trial Chamber and they say what they say, I don't need witnesses to refute their testimony. In order for me to refute witness Tanic, I have to bring two people; a person whose name I can't mention and Zoran Mijatovic . And both of them want to testify via videolink, and this can only be done if you allow that to happen. Now, how am I supposed to tell you how many witness I'm going to have? If you call any of the witnesses who you mentioned as the sources of hearsay evidence, at least as far as my client is concerned, I don't want to speak on behalf of the others if the others don't like it, I would really be very grateful if you did it. And if that happened, my job would be done. So my job can last between two weeks or two months. I have 20 witnesses at the moment. I can even give you their names, if they don't run away from me as they have a tendency to do. That's why I wanted to go to Belgrade, if you give me the time to go and chase my witnesses. I apologise for the joke. This is what I wanted to say: I'm kindly asking the Trial Chamber on my own behalf, on behalf of the Defence team to look at Article 98 and apply the Rule that you're entitled to apply and call these people because they will have to come. They will not be able to give them any excuses if you call them. And this is what I wanted to tell you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What's not clear, Mr. Fila, is how it makes a deference to the length of the case if we call these witnesses rather than you. It comes to the same thing surely.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In our country, it's not the same. The Trial Chamber is one level. If I call them, they can either say no. If you call them, they have to come. And those that you call will be those that will not have to appear on my list. That's what I'm saying. And if you call them, they will have to come. I'm sorry. I'm being very frank here. Maybe this is not very opportune, but that's the way I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There are two separate issues here. We can issue a subpoena to get them here and you can then lead them as witnesses, or we can issue a subpoena and then we can lead them as witnesses. But either -- either way, they're compelled to come in answer to the Trial Chamber's order.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right, Your Honour, but with your leave I would like to add something. If you're subpoenaed by you, they can be angry with you, but they will not go to Aberdeen to take it out against you. If I call them, if I subpoena them, then, well, they will come to me in Belgrade. This is what I'm saying. And I am usually very sincere in everything I say. It's not very useful all the time, but at the end of the day I believe this is the only way to go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You think I need a pseudonym, do you? Have we exhausted the Defence submissions? Mr. Bakrac?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know whether there is a need to hear all of us. I fully second everything that was said by my learned friends. I am astonished at the ability of Mr. Ackerman's team to be able to prepare in 120 days. This only by way of illustration to try and show you indeed how much time we need. The more time we are given in preparing our case the less the case will take. This case -- or, rather, the Prosecution case was foreseen to last for a year. As it turned out, it lasted for nine months. Of course, your role in that was essential, the people on the Bench, as well as on the side of the Prosecutor, but we also gave our own contribution. This was all with the goal of trying to prepare as efficiently as we can for our case. We learned along the way. I've sort of mentioned the 120 days in jest, but I really take this matter seriously. I second the request, because I believe it is essential for all of us. And this does not only apply to these three Defence teams that I have in mind in particular who came in late. The other three teams had a bit more time to prepare. They were in the case before us, but we're in the same boat. Primarily, however, I am speaking on behalf of the three teams who joined the case later. So as not to waste any of your time further, I wish to join everything said by my colleagues. And, of course, I wanted to stress yet again what Mr. Visnjic said. If I have a moment to get some information from Mr. Cvijic. Currently, we are processing 300 documents for translation. It is an important issue, because these documents appear depending on the sequence of witnesses and their testimonies. We procured those documents thinking that we can reply to those testimonies, and it is for our Defence teams only, the 300 documents. You should, I believe, bear that in mind, with all due respect as well, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Gosh, I thought we had exhausted the Lukic -- there must be on which the Lukic team don't have something to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I will be brief, Your Honour. Just for the sake of completeness, I agree with the comments of my colleagues especially the last three accused; and just wanted to add that with respect to ours, we'll be filing the written submission with specific details about technicalities. But one thing that we did want to stress is that with our -- we started the trial with 5 per cent of the documents that we knew of that we wanted to have and we're still receiving and going through those. With the pace of the trial, we've not able to process all of those. We also have translation issues, et cetera. The long and short of it is we right now foresee our list as 60 witness for the Defence and haven't yet decided whether those will be 92 ter or live. That's in flux, and it will change, obviously, given the preparations that we have to undertake. But at this stage, that's what we're looking at and we need to draw Your Honours' attention to the fact that we are in a unique position of being the only police defendants, which I think Your Honours are aware of and I think hopefully we've shown the amount of work that has been necessary to -- to prepare for the Prosecution's case. And we believe that just as diligent work will be required for the Defence case and, of course, the more time we have prior to that commencing, the better chance we have of making it run smoothly and efficiently and ensuring that justice is done for our client in particular and the proceedings, which are important in the greater scheme of things. So that is all. I'm completed and finished.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You'll bear in mind that while it will be for you to decide how to present your evidence, being realistic, decisions that we may make about the time that's available to you may compel you to tender evidence in writing that in a different situation you might have wanted to present orally. There can't be an open chequebook on this, and we have to find a way of being fair but also being expeditious as you'll appreciate.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I agree and I hope we have demonstrated a desire to try and be expeditious and diligent in terms of getting the witnesses for the Prosecution done. I can only say, at this stage, that we hope once Your Honours have the full information, which again several of our colleagues had already discussed preparing a written submission even prior to today and so we're in the process of putting one together and we will I think shortly have something to present all the factors for Your Honours' consideration, that we hope that we'll come up with a fair solution. But there are a lot of factors that need to be taken into account that need to be -- that need to be considered for purposes of making such a penultimate decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are you envisaging a written submission that actually tells us how long you think the presentation of your defence might take, or are you talking about some other technical detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, we can give estimates but for what weight -- how accurate those estimates are going to be - I am speaking now only for my team - we intend to give an estimate of what we believe our Defence case will take, based upon the number of witnesses and the documents that we anticipate utilising. And, again, I presume -- well, I'm not going to speak on behalf of the other teams. But the estimate may change, obviously, just as the estimates by the Prosecution have changed through the course of these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It sounds though as you might -- as though you may be further ahead with your preparation than some of the others.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I wish that were the case, Your Honour. Again, this is a wish list, and it's in flux, of the witnesses. Due to the pace of this case, we've actually had to call in at least one of our staff from Belgrade, who has been here full time with us, to try and keep up with this pace, so that we have really been working with a shortened staff in Belgrade, who have been trying to at least track down witnesses and get some preliminary information from them. But we really have not been able to sit down and to begin the intensive preparations that we believe are neglects in order to present a professional be a coherent defence in the manner that our client is entitled to and that indeed justice calls for.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We would also be taking account of the fact that there will be a summer recess. In the case of this trial, it's likely to be four weeks. We also take account of the fact that the further down the list of defendants you are the more time on the face of it you have to prepare. It may even be that among yourselves you would wish to select an order of presentation of Defence cases. But if you were to depart from the order that we have set up here, your clients would need to specifically approve of the way in which that was done because of the impact that evidence coming in a certain order could have on the respective accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, one of my main concerns, Mr. O'Sullivan mentioned I think four months after the ruling on the 98 bis for filing of their 65 ter list of witnesses and exhibits. My concern is that the amount of time between the filing of their 65 ter documents and the beginning of the case. We were required to file our 65 ters I think on the 10th of May and we started try on the 10th of July. There were two months between the receiving that information and the beginning of trial. We similarly would like to have some amount of time between the beginning of trial-- between the receipt of that information and the beginning of the Defence case to allow us to prepare and have a smooth -- as smooth as possible running of that phase of the case. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you help with the length of time you envisaged, if any, that preparing 98 bis submissions might take you? Because yours seems to me the harder job in that context it. All the Defence have to say is there's no evidence on X, Y, and Z, and you've got to find it. I mean, my inclination before listening to this today was have it the day after your evidence finished, because they should know now as we've gone along what there's no evidence on. And my inclination, I may also say, until listening today was it would be entirely oral. It would be done in a fairly summary way. It may be that certain accused here, and I'm trying to be as vague in this statement as possible, have a substantial 98 bis argument. And it may be others have a more or less technical argument about certain aspects of the indictment. But I would have thought that it was impossible for the Defence to be doing an adequate job, and they all appear to me to be doing that. It would be impossible to do that without having a clear notion of what the evidence is capable of proving against your individual clients. Preparation for the defence is another matter. And on that you can take it we have even no preliminary view, and we'll take account of all that's been said. But of course if 98 bis is dealt with quite quickly, then it makes it a bit easier to determine the other periods of time that are necessary. Mr. Ivetic, we're not particularly keen on having written submissions on this, unless you can identify for us that there is a specific benefit to be gained. What is it you feel you haven't had a chance to address?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Time frame, and there are some technical issues with respect to support staff, respect to access to electronic materials, and with respect to documents that we have been receiving and submitting for translation and some documents that are still in the process of being received. Just to give a full picture rather than going through all the nitty-gritty here, since we really did not have time to prepare for these arguments today. We had one hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: So we want to be coherent rather than taking up court time going through minutiae. That was the goal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But can I take it that you can do this pretty quickly?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I think so. I don't see anyone disagreeing. I think we can probably do it over the weekend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There may be assistance we can give on the question of translation. I don't know at the moment what the resource problems may amount to, but there's more than one way to skin a cat. And it may be that translation can be outsourced depending on the financial arrangements that can be made. I'm speaking off the top of my head just now, but the way we've made progress in this case has been on occasion to be innovative, rather than hide-bound by UN bureaucracy. And, therefore, if you are to address, as an example, the issue of translation, we'd like you to be positive about it and maybe tell us how the problem can be resolved rather than tell us we're going to be sitting around twiddling our thumbs for a month with no solution.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If I can give one example, there are a large number of our documents that the UN translators have refused to translate because they are not legible enough for them. So the solution has been we've seeking to get better copies of those documents, Your Honour. I don't know. They are legible to be B/C/S readers. My staff and myself can read them, but apparently they're not legible enough for the electronic translation system to accept them. So we've had several documents rejected on that score that we're trying to get better copies of. There might be another solution to that, there might be. I don't know. But we've been trying to do what we thought was the reasonable aspect of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We've so far been very fortunate in this case that very considerable efforts have been made by CLSS to favour the progress of this case, but we also recognise that the workload has increased because of the number of ongoing cases. And in that context, it's I think incumbent on all of us to try to work out a way of helping each other to make progress.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's true. And I might add that I know from at least from our experience, CLSS has been working very diligently in terms of translating documents that we needed for cross, so that we have been able to get official translations of documents for cross purposes rather quickly. But, of course, that is taking them away from documents that we would need in the Defence case, which some or the same documents and some are not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You'll get no criticism from us for occasionally having reduced the extent to which you require translation of a document a little too far and finding that you have to refer to something untranslated. We'd rather see you do that than have large quantities of material unnecessarily translated, which is a temptation because you may find yourself under pressure to make decisions quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's something we -- we feel on our Defence team very strongly about, because we have been trying to organise documents. And we believe that might end up with groups of documents that are of similar nature, and so we -- one of our proposed solutions might be that we ask to tender exemplars of a particular set translated and then the rest of the documents untranslated that are of the same nature or talk about the same things. So that is something we do have in mind, and we're going to be working with everyone to try and find a solution because we do definitely foresee the need not to overburden the translation system with documents we may not need or that are duplicative of one another.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Where only a very short passage is are involved, then the translation can be done in the court. Now, as far as next week is concerned, and this unprecedented generosity must not be misinterpreted - Mr. Hannis isn't even going to get a yellow card for this one - we will grant the Prosecution motion and adjourn until a week on Monday. I hope -- that's a week when we're sitting 9.00 to 3.30. I hope that we'll get a proposed list of witnesses earlier than Thursday of this coming week, and we will do our best to clear the decks of outstanding motions in the course of next week, and hopefully that will include a decision on the future conduct of the case, which may not be entirely in line with the requests that have been made today. But we will give serious consideration to what's been proposed in the course of the next few days. We will anticipate that any written supplementary submissions that you wish to make will be in our hands by Tuesday.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That should be fine, Your Honour. And I think it will probably be a joint submission, so it will be one submission for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And it is not a submission that requires a response. It requires a response. But, obviously, if Mr. Hannis feels the need to respond then he would do so, or at least indicate to us that he intends to do so more or less immediately, because we are liable to make decisions fairly quickly in the course of next week. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm wondering if -- I don't know if this is possible for Mr. Hannis to do, but the efficiency of our use of time next week would be dramatically enhanced if we could get at least an indication of the order in which the rest of the witnesses will be coming, so we'll be -- we can be working on those that will be coming in the first two or three weeks at least as we restart, and I think that would enhance our preparation and enhance the possibility of moving at the speed we want to move.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, you can please discuss that when we rise just now, and hopefully Mr. Hannis can accommodate you. So we'll resume on Monday the 19th at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 19th day of February, 2007, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 2.37 p.m.,
